claims.statement: For a hot drop, pre-created seats taken by compare-and-set or SKIP LOCKED (P3 CAS, P2 skip-locked) sell 4-8x faster than any single counter row, but only with retry backoff in mind, and a counter on the event row also blocks unrelated edits to it. Both deliberately wrong controls fired in the same run. Two replications thirteen days later, on the same topology and with the design order reversed between them (AB/BA), reproduced the range - P3 at 4.30-7.06x and 4.64-6.99x, P2 at 3.25-5.25x and 5.78-8.71x against the two counters - while every absolute throughput fell 26-72% below the original run. The range is therefore the claim and the absolute numbers are one session's readings.
limits: one run of the experiment, a single measurement per configuration
the run has 42 cells of which 2 failed (C2 count (SER) on the two YugabyteDB topologies); those cells are not evidence

every absolute throughput in the 2026-09-26 replication was 26-72% below the 2026-09-13 run for the same design and tier, so the 4-8x range reproduced while the numbers behind it did not; the range is quotable and the figures are not

the ratio moved between runs: p3 against c4 went 7.07 to 4.37 to 4.64 at 100 seats and 7.26 to 4.30 to 4.70 at 1000, and p2 against c4 went 3.97 to 3.25 to 5.78, so the range is a range, not a point, and individual ratios shift by up to 44%

the replication re-ran neither deliberately wrong control (c1_count_naive, h0_hold_naive_confirm), so it strengthens the comparison without re-firing the correctness control that the first run provided

r1_inventory_row recorded one trial of about 4x lower throughput than its siblings at each tier (122 and 117 against 468-653); whether that is a real instability or a harness artefact is unresolved, and r1 is the weakest comparison in the replication
two of the original sweep's five tiers (10 and 10000 seats) were not re-measured

p2_precreated_skip_locked moved 58-76% between the two same-day replications while the counters moved within 15% and p3 within 7%; it ran first in one and last in the other, so that design carries a position or warm-up effect as large as the comparison it takes part in, and the claim's pairing of p2 with p3 hides it - the >=3x result holds at both extremes

the anomalous r1_inventory_row trials of the first replication (122 and 117 against 468-653) did not recur in the reverse-order run, which makes a harness artefact likelier than a design property without settling it

the read phase of this claim's primary anchor 20260913T021206Z was client-CPU throttled by a design-dependent amount (0.2 s for p2_precreated_skip_locked to 29.5 s for h0_hold_naive_confirm, out of 633 CFS periods), so that report's read figures are not quotable. The hazard reproduces on the current harness (20260929T165533Z, 20260929T170353Z: r1_inventory_row loses 420 of 634 and 422 of 633 periods), and the 2026-09-30 budget calibration (20260930T000544Z, 20260930T000759Z, 20260930T001013Z) shows the client's quota is a symptom rather than the ceiling: at three client cores the client is not throttled at all and the reads are slower (52,884 -> 43,726 ops/s at 10 seats), because the third core comes out of the database's share of the machine's four CPUs (database throttled periods 238 -> 847 -> 1052). The claim's own basis is the race phase (sell rate), where one cell in fourteen designs shows throttling. The read family has since been re-measured at the study's new 2-worker read footprint (20260930T164028Z, 20260930T164834Z: four designs, client unthrottled at 0 of ~631 periods, every cell latency-bound at 2.00 operations in flight for 2 workers (with the mean latency; a median-based count reads 1.9)), so read levels are quotable only with the footprint attached. All fifteen designs now have a footprint-2 footing (the four-design tranche plus the eleven-design tranche 20260930T201732Z/20260930T203913Z, where no design throttles: 0 of ~631 periods in all 22 read phases), and this claim's primary anchor's own footprint-8 read figures remain not quotable: the inflation they carry is design-dependent, 1.09x to 2.22x, and it tracks how many periods the old client lost per design rather than anything about the designs. All fifteen designs have since been measured in a **single run**, twice and in reversed order (20261001T100948Z, 20261001T103931Z): 0 throttled periods in all 30 read phases and every one of the 270 cells store-bound at 2.00 operations in flight by the mean latency, so the family's levels are jointly comparable within that session. Two consequences for quoting: the top group (h0, h1, r1, r2, p4) differs by 4%, inside that session's own order term, so its internal ranking is not quotable - only the 1.5x gap between that group and the per-seat group is; and c1_count_naive carries a 40% position term (first of one order against last of the other), so its q01 level should not be quoted from these runs.

claims.statement: A ticketing database chosen only to prevent overbooking cannot report refunds at all: in 14 of 15 designs the refunds report (r05) is unanswerable and the sales/revenue (r01) and last-purchase (r03) reports are wrong across a refund, reproduced in two whole runs in both design orders on PostgreSQL at scale small, with the append-only ledger (X1 CAS+ledger) the only design that answers r05. The ledger's storage cost depends on which relations are counted and moves about a percentage point between runs: about 33-35% more than P3 by table size (33.4% and 34.8% in the two runs, 35.2% in the primary), about 35-36% counting every relation (35.0% and 35.9% in the two runs, 36.2% in the primary), and 37.4-37.9% by index size alone.
limits: answerability is a schema fact, not a timing
the +33-35% storage delta is a relation-size difference measured in the primary run and deterministic for the same dataset and design; it is not a repeated timed result
the P3 -> X1 read rows of this run are excluded, because the difference belongs to the configuration as a whole rather than to one decision inside it

the read phase of this claim's primary anchor 20260920T234953Z was client-CPU throttled by a design-dependent amount (2.3 s for p2_precreated_skip_locked to 58.1 s for r1_inventory_row, out of about 1085 CFS periods), so that report's read figures are not quotable: the hazard reproduces on the current harness (20260929T165533Z, 20260929T170353Z: r1_inventory_row 32.3 s of ~63 s of periods, both orders), and the 2026-09-30 budget calibration shows the client's quota is a symptom rather than the ceiling - the read level on this machine is set by the database's share of four CPUs, and adding a client core removes the client's throttling while making the reads slower. Answerability and the r05 storage/speed result are unaffected: the ledger still answers r05 at 30.3k and 33.0k ops/s against the primary's 32.2k, and at the new 2-worker read footprint the r05 result reproduces independently at 32,164 ops/s (20260930T164028Z), so that number has a footprint-2 footing; all fifteen designs now have one (the eleven-design tranche 20260930T201732Z/20260930T203913Z adds the rest, unthrottled), while this claim's primary anchor's own footprint-8 read figures remain not quotable (design-dependent inflation, 1.09x to 2.22x). **Correction, 2026-09-30: an earlier caveat here said the two many-row queries (q02_band_events, q05_band_tickets_sold) had client-bound levels; it is withdrawn.** A one-worker tranche (20260930T232926Z, 20260930T233744Z) shows that in-flight measured with the **mean** latency is exactly 1.000 in all 72 cells at one worker and 2.00 at two, so every read cell in the family is a store measurement at a stated footprint, and only its magnitude depends on the concurrency. Two errors produced the withdrawn caveat: q05 does not return 28 rows (all three variants return one - COUNT/SUM with no GROUP BY), and in-flight computed from the **median** understates the concurrency by the latency skew (mean/p50 up to 2.7x), which reads exactly like a worker idling between fetches. The primary anchor's **PostgreSQL read cells have since been re-stated** on the footprint-2 footing (analysis 20261001T-read-cells-restated: all fifteen designs, both orders, every cell store-bound at 2.00 operations in flight), so its `pg-single` read figures may be replaced rather than caveated. All fifteen designs have since been measured in a **single run**, twice and in reversed order (20261001T100948Z, 20261001T103931Z): 0 throttled periods in all 30 read phases and every one of the 270 cells store-bound at 2.00 operations in flight by the mean latency, so the family's levels are jointly comparable within that session. Two consequences for quoting: the top group (h0, h1, r1, r2, p4) differs by 4%, inside that session's own order term, so its internal ranking is not quotable - only the 1.5x gap between that group and the per-seat group is; and c1_count_naive carries a 40% position term (first of one order against last of the other), so its q01 level should not be quoted from these runs. Its two **YugabyteDB read arms have no replacement** and remain an explicit coverage gap

the storage percentage depends on the rule and on the page layout, and must not be quoted as one number: tables only 33.4-35.2%, every relation 35.0-36.2%, indexes alone 37.7%; the same pair's relation sizes moved 0.26% (p3) and 0.41% (x1) between two runs 29 minutes apart, so the delta moved 0.9 percentage points; the index-only figure spans 37.4-37.9% across the five runs, so even there the rule is a band and not a point, and the 2026-10-02 replication's M4 (reproducible within 1%) is falsified by that movement - a tighter figure would need a vacuumed comparison, which is a different measurement

the answerability statuses are the harness's own audit of its own schema, computed as a pure function of the design and emitted inside the read phase; the 2026-10-02 replication therefore tests reproducibility across two whole runs and not the independence of the audit's rule, and it re-measured no timing

claims.statement: At 128 buyers the append-only ledger's cost over compare-and-set rises with the size of the event rather than sitting in one band: on PostgreSQL it is about 1.1x at 10 seats (where the direction is not reliable), about 1.2-1.4x at 100-1000 seats, about 1.8x at 10000 seats and about 2.5x at 100000 seats, measured in twelve whole runs in both design orders, with wide spreads at the small tiers. The 1.8-2.2x on YugabyteDB, the 2.1-2.5x on the refund itself and the up-to-5x delay to the organiser's own edit are single-run figures that have not been re-measured, and no design ever under-booked a seat.

scoped to 128 buyers; must not be extrapolated to 32 buyers
single run, three trials per tier

replicated on 2026-09-27 in both design orders at 128 buyers, three trials per tier: the p3/x1 ratio came out 1.53x, 1.71x and 2.00x at 100, 1000 and 10000 seats in the first order and 0.99x, 1.30x and 1.74x in the reversed order, so the ratios reproduce in size while the lowest of them falls below this claim's 1.1x floor

the ordering is not stable at the smallest tier: CAS read 4163 against the ledger's 2724 at 100 seats in the first order (1.53x) and 3588 against 3618 in the reversed order (0.99x), i.e. the ledger marginally faster - so the designs swap places at a fixed buyer count, which is what v2-09 records for changing buyer counts

the former 'tight spreads' wording did not hold at that tier: the 100-seat cell spread 57% for CAS and 37% for the ledger in the first order, and 47% and 51% in the reversed order, while every other tier stayed within 4-17% - and because the wide spread appeared at the same tier in both orders it belongs to the cell rather than to a design's position in the session

re-scoped on 2026-09-27 (HIGH, task repo/v2-08-rescope): the flat 1.1-2.3x band and the words 'tight spreads' were removed from the statement because the cost measured across the tier axis is monotone (about 1.1x at 10 seats to about 2.5x at 100000) and the small-tier cells spread 47-77%; the superseded wording, the evidence behind each change, and the earlier post-v6 re-scopings of v2-06 and v2-11, are recorded in book/evidence/v6/SUPERSESSION_LEDGER.md

the earlier 'single run, three trials per tier' limit describes the primary run only; the claim now rests on 8 whole runs (2 at 3 trials across 3 tiers, then 6 at 5 trials across the 100- and 1000-seat tiers)

settled on 2026-09-27 by a third tranche of six runs (5 fresh-load trials per cell, three in each design order): the 100-seat p3/x1 run median was 1.279, 1.333, 1.257, 1.712, 1.328 and 1.476, so the single 0.99x reading of the reversed replication does not reproduce and the former band is not widened by this evidence; the ledger was slower in 29 of the 30 individual trial pairs (pooled per-trial median ratio 1.391x, range 0.940-1.920)

the former 'tight spreads' wording still failed at the 100-seat tier across all eight runs: the cell's spread was 47-77% for CAS and 26-54% for the ledger in the six settle runs, and the run-to-run spread of the tier-100 ratio is 34% over those six and 54% over all eight (0.992-1.712, median 1.331), so that tier supports a direction and not a point ratio

the 1000-seat positive control read 1.304-1.712 in all six settle runs, so the harness detected the ledger's cost in every run; correctness was green throughout (46/46 P3, 48/48 X1 verifications, 0 over-booked, 0 under-booked, 0 timed-out), and no settle cell is void

the tier axis was then measured on 2026-09-27 in four more whole runs (5 trials per cell, two runs in each design order, all five tiers measured in every run): the pooled run-median p3/x1 rose 1.075, 1.237, 1.409, 1.845 and 2.505 at 10, 100, 1000, 10000 and 100000 seats, monotone in the pooled medians and in every individual run, so the ledger's cost is a function of tier and the claim's former 1.1-2.3x band described its middle three tiers rather than the whole axis

the statement's YugabyteDB, refund and organiser-edit figures come from the primary run alone and are labelled as not re-measured; the replication programme covered only the PostgreSQL race, so nothing here re-measures them, and v2-09's finding that the design order moves the ratio at the small sizes still applies

both endpoint tiers lie outside the former band and had never been repeated before this tranche: at 10 seats the run medians were 1.023-1.180 (pooled 1.075, below its 1.1x floor) while the per-trial median was 1.131 and the ledger was slower in only 12 of 20 trial pairs, so the cost there sits at the floor and its direction flips in 40% of trials; at 100000 seats the ledger was slower in 20 of 20 pairs (pooled per-trial median 2.456, run medians 2.249-2.637), above the 2.3x top

the 100000-seat tier is a single event per trial, so its 20 trial pairs are 20 readings of one event and an event-specific effect would be indistinguishable from a tier effect; the 10-seat cell is near-degenerate (100 events of 10 seats against 128 buyers) and its cells spread 16-71%

correctness was green in all four tier-axis runs (0 over-booked, 0 under-booked, 0 timed-out, 0 errors); with the two earlier tranches the tier-100 reading now rests on twelve runs whose run medians span 0.992-1.712 (median 1.331, spread 54%), so that tier still offers a direction rather than a point ratio

claims.statement: On PostgreSQL the ledger is slower than compare-and-set at 1,000 seats at every buyer count tested, 8 to 128, and in both design orders (55 of 55 trial pairs over eleven runs), so the two designs do not change places with the load: the primary run's apparent swap came from its own confound, buyer count and design order having moved together. The size of the cost does vary without a simple trend (about 1.2-1.3x near 16-32 buyers and 1.4-1.9x at 64-128; one 8-buyer cell changed state mid-run), and the design order moves absolute throughput several-fold without changing which design is faster. On YugabyteDB the primary run's own range is 1.7-5.7x, wider than a headline would quote.
limits: the stable direction is measured at 1,000 seats across 8-128 buyers and at 32 buyers across all five tiers; the buyer-count axis is not swept at the other four tiers, so the full buyer x tier surface is open

one primary run per (buyers, order) cell, with a reference cell that moved 8.6% between the two ends of the tranche, so a level whose two orders differ by more than that is placed by the ratio and not by the absolutes

claims.statement: Under one hot key, a bounded-retry version check (c1_optimistic_version) and a lock-before-update (c2_pessimistic_lock) cross over between one and two concurrent writers: the lock delivers 0.89x the version check's throughput at 1 writer (1,177 against 1,329 ops/s) and 1.10x at 2 writers (1,285 against 1,167), rising to 1.68x at 32 writers (877 against 523) and 1.60x at 64, while the version check's own throughput falls 2.9x across the sweep (1,329 to 466 ops/s) and its conflict count rises from 0 to 21,301.
limits: PostgreSQL single node, small scale, one hot key, one measurement per level across seven runs (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 writers), so the curve carries no spread at any level

we tested the obvious explanation for the lock's advantage and it failed: with the retry budget set to zero the c2/c1 ratio at 16 writers is 1.60 against 1.61 with retries, and c2_pessimistic_lock, which never retries either way, moved by the same 10% as c1 between the two same-day runs, so the advantage cannot be put down to retry work (analysis 20260926T-retry-control, runs 20260926T142926Z and 20260926T143014Z)
the seven runs used two phase sets (the first four also ran read and write phases); the contention metric should not depend on that, but it is an assumption rather than a measurement
no negative control in this sweep; control_coverage is recorded absent rather than implied
the 1-writer point is the edge of the sweep, so the optimistic side is bracketed by one level only
absolute numbers are a laptop comparison; the shape of the curve is what transfers
absolute throughput is day-specific: c2 measured 869 ops/s on 2026-09-23 and 1,056 on 2026-09-26 at identical settings, phases and writer count, so only the within-run ratio is carried across days

run_level.source: the seven contention reports in this sweep
run_level.note: No negative control ran in this sweep; the lost-update control belongs to the v2 tranche and is not reused as evidence here.

support.expected: 1,329 ops/s at 1 writer falling to 466 at 64

attribution.note: c1 and c2 differ in one decision: whether the current row is guarded by a version check or by a lock.

crossover.dimension: concurrent writers on one hot key

claims.statement: Crossing who maintains the parent rollup (trigger n3_rollup_trigger against application n4_rollup_app) with the size of a replacement (10, 60 and 240 entries per installed product) shows the maintenance penalty is a function of size rather than a constant: across 7, 9 and 7 runs at the three sizes the application design delivers roughly 1.1-3.2x the trigger design on whole-configuration replacement at 10 entries, 2.5-9.0x at 60 and 10-24x at 240, the ordering by size holding in every arrangement measured, and no rollup mismatch is recorded at any size.
limits: PostgreSQL single node, small scale, one measurement per tier across 10, 60 and 240 entries per installed product, so the curve carries no spread at any level
one operation only: w05_replace_all replaces the whole configuration, and a workload that appends a single entry would sit at the low end of this curve at any size
the axis is capped by the small scale at 240 entries and the curve is still rising steeply there, so nothing here bounds where it flattens
no negative control in these three runs; control_coverage is recorded absent rather than implied
two designs cannot separate the two mechanisms that predict this shape: the trigger fires once per row written, and its per-row work may also be heavier than the application's single statement

at 60 entries per installation the three runs give a median of 3.42x, about 22% below the 4.38x the first run recorded and below the 3.99-5.69x v2-13 replicated for the same operation, so the corroboration of v2-13 here is approximate - same operation, same size, same direction - and not a match

the ratio at each size is a band describing what has been seen, not a range a future reading must fall inside: 7 runs at 10 entries span 1.06-3.15x, 9 at 60 span 2.51-8.95x and 7 at 240 span 10.20-24.20x, and the two lower bands touch when everything is pooled (3.15 against 2.51) even though every individual arrangement ordered them correctly

arrangement in time decides what a repeat can see: three runs of a size placed next to each other in the session agreed within 15-55%, while the same three runs spread across the session (a Latin square) spread by about 100% - the sequential layout understated the uncertainty because adjacent runs share the session's state

a reference cell measured immediately before and after this tranche moved 445 to 640 ops/s, +44%, so the session was not a stable instrument and the drift it produced is measured rather than inferred; the reference is a different operation from the one compared here and bounds the movement without being its exact size
a band built from six runs did not contain a seventh: tier 10 measured 1.06 against the 1.34-3.15 range the earlier tranches had established

the session does not drift in one direction, it wanders: three readings of one reference cell taken through a single tranche gave 8.64, 5.21 and 8.53, so reading only the start and the end of that tranche would have reported no movement while the middle sat 39% below both

the ratio is more portable than the absolute numbers: over those same three reference readings the ratio spread 40% against 49% for the application design's throughput and 114% for the trigger's, because a session term shared by both designs cancels in the ratio

run_level.source: the three tier reports (2 designs x 3 tiers)
run_level.note: No negative control in this tranche; the rollup drift control belongs to the v2 tranche and is not reused as evidence here.

attribution.note: The maintenance decision is the only difference between the two designs; the replacement size is the only difference between the tiers. Both factors are varied independently, which is what makes this an interaction rather than a package.
